::: why
**Why this part:** the decade lines say *whether* a name was popular in a decade, but one name can be popular in several. To answer Q2 sharply we want one number for how old a name is. To answer Q3 we want the actual names that differ between areas. Before trusting any pattern, we check that it does not depend on how we define a "human name" (Q4).

**Transforms:** grouping, lookup (left join), wider, longer, extracting, recoding, aggregates.
:::

## How old is each name?
The **namesake year** (built in Part 5) is the average birth year of everyone with a name, with each year counted once per baby. Four familiar names show what it measures.
```{r}
#| label: namesake-examples
ssa_name_totals |>
  filter(name == "DOROTHY" | name == "JENNIFER" | name == "LUNA" | name == "MAX") |>
  arrange(namesake_year)
```

```{r}
#| label: name-age-facts
#| include: false
namesake <- function(n) {
  ssa_name_totals |>
    filter(name == n) |>
    summarize(year = round(namesake_year)) |>
    unlist()
}
```

::: takeaway
The average Dorothy was born in `r namesake("DOROTHY")`, the average Jennifer in `r namesake("JENNIFER")` and the average Luna in `r namesake("LUNA")`, so one number captures a name's generation.
:::

## Do richer areas choose older names? (Q2)
For each area we average the namesake year of dogs with a common human name. A common human name has at least 100 births in total, which is stricter than appearing in the SSA records at all: a name given to five babies in one year is not a common human name. Then we compare income groups and test the link across areas.
```{r}
#| label: name-ages-by-area
area_name_ages <- dogs_by_income_group |>
  mutate(human_name = total_births >= 100) |>
  group_by(zcta, income_group) |>
  summarize(
    median_income = first(income),
    human_name_dogs = sum(human_name),
    human_name_share = mean(human_name),
    namesake_year = mean(namesake_year[human_name]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

area_name_ages |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  summarize(
    areas = n(),
    human_name_share = mean(human_name_share),
    namesake_year = mean(namesake_year)
  )
```

To test whether the link between income and name age could be chance, we use a correlation test across areas. Income is very skewed, so we use its logarithm.
```{r}
#| label: namesake-test
namesake_test <- cor.test(log(area_name_ages$median_income), area_name_ages$namesake_year)
namesake_test
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-namesake-year
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
area_name_ages |>
  ggplot(aes(x = median_income, y = namesake_year)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = human_name_dogs, colour = human_name_share), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "#6b46c1") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_percent(), end = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Do richer areas give dogs older human names?",
    subtitle = "Average birth year of people who share the dog's name; one point per NYC area",
    x = "Median household income, ACS 2024 (log scale)",
    y = "Average namesake birth year",
    size = "Dogs with a\nhuman name", colour = "Share of\nhuman names"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: takeaway
The correlation between log income and namesake year is `r round(namesake_test$estimate, 2)` (p = `r format.pval(namesake_test$p.value, digits = 2)`). `r if (namesake_test$estimate < 0) "Richer areas lean toward older human names." else "Richer areas do not lean toward older human names."`
:::

## Which names set rich and poor areas apart? (Q3)
The most popular names are popular everywhere, so we compare each name's *share* of dogs in the richest group with its share in the poorest:

1. Count dogs per name in Q1 and Q5, then go **wider** so the two counts sit side by side. A name missing from one group gets 0.
2. Turn counts into shares of each group, and divide the Q5 share by the Q1 share. A ratio of 2 means "twice as common in the richest areas". We add 1 to each count so a 0 does not break the division, and keep names with at least 30 dogs.
3. **Look up** the decade in which each name ranked highest (its peak decade) and **recode** it into an era label.
```{r}
#| label: distinctive-names
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
peak_decades <- ssa_decades |>
  group_by(name) |>
  slice_max(n = 1, order_by = -rank, with_ties = FALSE) |>   # best rank = peak decade
  ungroup() |>
  select(name, peak_decade = decade)

distinctive_names <- dogs_by_income_group |>
  filter(income_group == "Q1 lowest income" | income_group == "Q5 highest income") |>
  count(income_group, name) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = income_group, values_from = n) |>
  rename(q1_dogs = `Q1 lowest income`, q5_dogs = `Q5 highest income`) |>
  mutate(q1_dogs = replace_na(q1_dogs, 0), q5_dogs = replace_na(q5_dogs, 0)) |>
  filter(q1_dogs + q5_dogs >= 30) |>
  mutate(
    q1_share = (q1_dogs + 1) / sum(q1_dogs + 1),
    q5_share = (q5_dogs + 1) / sum(q5_dogs + 1)
  ) |>
  mutate(rich_to_poor_ratio = q5_share / q1_share) |>
  left_join(ssa_name_totals |> select(name, total_births), by = "name") |>
  left_join(peak_decades, by = "name") |>
  mutate(name_type = case_when(
    is.na(total_births) | total_births < 100 ~ "not a common human name",
    peak_decade < 1950 ~ "human name, peaked before 1950",
    peak_decade < 1990 ~ "human name, peaked 1950–1989",
    .default = "human name, peaked 1990 or later"
  ))

distinctive_top <- bind_rows(
  distinctive_names |> slice_max(n = 10, order_by = rich_to_poor_ratio, with_ties = FALSE),
  distinctive_names |> slice_max(n = 10, order_by = -rich_to_poor_ratio, with_ties = FALSE)
)

distinctive_top |>
  mutate(name = fct_reorder(str_to_title(name), rich_to_poor_ratio)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rich_to_poor_ratio, y = name, fill = name_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "human name, peaked before 1950" = "#6b46c1",
    "human name, peaked 1950–1989" = "#a0aec0",
    "human name, peaked 1990 or later" = "#2c7a7b",
    "not a common human name" = "#ed8936"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Most over-represented names in the richest vs poorest areas",
    x = "Share in richest fifth ÷ share in poorest fifth (log scale)",
    y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: distinctive-facts
#| include: false
rich_side <- distinctive_top |> filter(rich_to_poor_ratio > 1) |> arrange(desc(rich_to_poor_ratio))
poor_side <- distinctive_top |> filter(rich_to_poor_ratio < 1) |> arrange(rich_to_poor_ratio)
```

::: takeaway
The richest areas over-represent names such as `r str_c(str_to_title(head(rich_side$name, 5)), collapse = ", ")`; the poorest over-represent names such as `r str_c(str_to_title(head(poor_side$name, 5)), collapse = ", ")`. `r sum(rich_side$name_type == "human name, peaked before 1950")` of the 10 rich-side names peaked before 1950, against `r sum(poor_side$name_type == "human name, peaked before 1950")` on the poor side.
:::

## Does our definition of a human name matter? (Q4)
Part 5 counts a name as human if it appears in the SSA records at all (5+ births in some year); this part used 100 births. We check four thresholds at once: one **aggregate** column per threshold for each income group, then go **longer** and **extract** the threshold number from the column name.
```{r}
#| label: threshold-check
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
threshold_check <- dogs_by_income_group |>
  group_by(income_group) |>
  summarize(
    births_5 = mean(total_births >= 5),
    births_100 = mean(total_births >= 100),
    births_1000 = mean(total_births >= 1000),
    births_5000 = mean(total_births >= 5000)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(births_5, births_100, births_1000, births_5000), names_to = "rule", values_to = "human_name_share") |>
  separate_wider_delim(rule, delim = "_", names = c("label", "threshold")) |>
  mutate(threshold = as.numeric(threshold))

threshold_check |>
  ggplot(aes(x = threshold, y = human_name_share, colour = income_group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title = "Does the income gap depend on our threshold?",
    x = "Births needed to count as a human name (log scale)",
    y = "Dogs with a human name", colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-facts
#| include: false
threshold_gaps <- threshold_check |>
  filter(income_group == "Q1 lowest income" | income_group == "Q5 highest income") |>
  select(threshold, income_group, human_name_share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = income_group, values_from = human_name_share) |>
  mutate(gap = `Q5 highest income` - `Q1 lowest income`)

gap_is_stable <- all(threshold_gaps$gap > 0) | all(threshold_gaps$gap < 0)
```

::: takeaway
The gap between the richest and poorest groups ranges from `r round(100 * min(threshold_gaps$gap), 1)` to `r round(100 * max(threshold_gaps$gap), 1)` percentage points across the four thresholds. `r if (gap_is_stable) "A stricter threshold lowers every rate, but the gap keeps the same direction, so the comparison does not depend on where we draw the line." else "The gap changes direction across thresholds, so the result depends on how we define a human name."`
:::
